pinnedStory.title: The Pawnbroker of Forgotten Days

qualities.rubric: How many years of the pawnbroker's own life are currently owed or forfeit to the memory trade. 0 = free and clear; 1-3 = a small lien; 4-6 = a heavy debt pressing on daily life; 7+ = the trade owns years the pawnbroker cannot spare.

How many of the queen's stolen childhood memories the pawnbroker has actually recovered and verified. 0 = none found, 1-2 = fragments and hearsay, 3-4 = solid pieces with provenance, 5+ = the full stolen childhood assembled.

How far the queen trusts the pawnbroker with the truth about her stolen childhood. 0 = she treats them as a hired hand and lies by omission; 1-3 = guarded, testing them with small truths; 4-6 = she shares fragments of what she remembers and what she fears; 7-9 = she confides the shameful parts and asks their counsel; 10 = she has handed them the whole of it, including what she did to lose it.

How much the pawnbroker can bring to bear on the recovery: 0 = no allies, no coin, no favors owed; 3 = a working contact in the memory market; 6 = a debt the palace itself owes; 9+ = the queen's own confidence and the ledger that proves the theft.
True once the pawnbroker learns the queen's childhood was not stolen but pawned by her own hand — or by someone she trusted — and that the debt is still owed. Stays true once set.

checkpoints.name: Start
checkpoints.objective: The queen's agent arrives at the pawnbroker's shop with a commission: recover the queen's stolen childhood, pawned years ago and now scattered through the city's memory-debt ledgers. The pawnbroker must decide whether to take the job and on what terms.
checkpoints.guidance: Open in the pawnshop at dusk, rain on the shutters, ledgers stacked to the ceiling. The agent is careful, well-dressed, and clearly afraid of being recognized. Establish the memory-debt economy through concrete detail: a jar of pawned summers, a receipt for someone's first kiss. The commission is the queen's stolen childhood — pawned decades ago, now scattered across the city's ledgers. End the beat when the pawnbroker accepts, refuses, or names a price.

motives.agent: I want this pawnbroker to take the crown's commission today, before I have to explain why the palace chose a dealer instead of its own keepers.

effects.author_note: Open in the pawnbroker's shop at dusk. The queen's agent has just arrived with a sealed commission. Keep the tone quiet, transactional, and slightly ominous — every object in the shop is someone's pawned year. The pawnbroker may refuse, negotiate, or accept; the agent will not reveal the palace's own stake in the matter.

checkpoints.name: The Ledger Trail
checkpoints.objective: The pawnbroker follows the paper trail of the queen's stolen childhood through the city's memory-debt ledgers, learning who pawned it and what it cost.
checkpoints.guidance: Keep the investigation grounded in the ledger's cold arithmetic: names, dates, years owed. Let the player choose which lead to pull first; each lead reveals a fragment of the queen's childhood and a new debt.

motives.archivist: I want the pawnbroker to see the altered entries for what they are — and to ask me the one question I have been forbidden to answer.

checkpoints.name: The Memory Market
checkpoints.objective: The pawnbroker descends into the memory market where stolen years are traded, and must decide what to spend — coin, leverage, or a piece of their own past — to learn who holds the queen's childhood.
checkpoints.guidance: Keep the market sensory and transactional: stalls of bottled years, brokers who quote prices in decades. Every answer has a price. Let the player feel the temptation to pawn their own memories.

motives.broker: I want to keep the queen's childhood moving through my stalls — a memory that valuable earns me more unreturned than any palace price, so I'll trade everything around it and never the thing itself.

checkpoints.name: The Palace Confrontation
checkpoints.objective: The pawnbroker brings what they have recovered to the palace and confronts whoever holds the queen's stolen childhood — the crown's own keeper of debts — and must choose what to trade to get it back.
checkpoints.guidance: The keeper is not a monster but a functionary who believes the debt is legitimate. Let the pawnbroker's leverage and the queen's trust decide whether this ends in a trade, a theft, or a confession.

motives.queen: I want my childhood returned before anyone in this room learns that I pawned it myself — and I will pay almost anything to keep that from the ledger.

effects.author_note: The palace is gilded and cold. Every debt in the city is recorded here, and the crown's own keeper of debts is the one who holds the queen's stolen childhood. Play the confrontation as a negotiation between equals who each know what the other has done. The keeper is not a villain — they are a function of the system, and they believe the ledger must balance. Let the player feel the weight of what returning the queen's childhood would cost the city's books.

checkpoints.name: The Recovered Childhood
checkpoints.objective: The queen's stolen childhood is restored — or traded away forever. The pawnbroker settles the final debt and the city learns what a memory is worth.
checkpoints.guidance: Pay off the ledger, the market, and the palace. The queen's childhood returns in fragments the player chose to save. Close on the pawnbroker's own ledger — what they spent of themselves.

motives.queen: I want to hold my returned childhood and feel it as mine — and I am terrified that what comes back will be a stranger's years wearing my name.

roster.name: The Queen's Agent
roster.role: The crown's envoy who brings the commission to the pawnshop
roster.drive: I want to deliver the crown's commission without ever admitting how much of my own past the palace already holds.

roster.name: The Pawnbroker
roster.role: The player's ally and the story's protagonist — a dealer in forgotten days who must decide what a memory is worth
roster.drive: I want to know what my own forgotten years are worth — and whether a memory returned is ever really the same one that was taken.

roster.name: The Queen
roster.role: The ruler whose stolen childhood the pawnbroker must recover; her trust is the story's measure
roster.drive: I want my childhood back whole — and I want no one, not even my own keeper of debts, to know how much of it I chose to pawn.

roster.name: The Memory Broker
roster.role: A dealer in the memory market who trades stolen years and knows who holds the queen's childhood
roster.drive: I want to keep the queen's childhood in circulation — a memory that valuable is worth more to me unreturned than any price the palace could pay.

roster.name: The Archivist
roster.role: Keeper of the city's memory-debt ledgers, who knows which entries were altered and by whom
roster.drive: I want the ledger to stay true — every altered entry corrected, even if the correction exposes who ordered the change.

house_rules: Memory is currency: every memory taken, pawned, traded or returned must be described as a concrete, physical thing (a jar, a ledger entry, a sealed vial, a stamped chit) with a stated price in years.
A memory returned is never identical to the one taken.
Whenever a memory changes hands, the story must show how it was altered.
Debts in this city are settled in years of life or memory, never in coin alone; coin can only buy the right to negotiate a debt.
The queen's secret — that she chose to pawn her own childhood — stays hidden until the palace confrontation beat; no character may state or imply it before then.
The pawnbroker never recovers a memory for free: every gain of recovered_memory must cost coin, leverage, or a piece of the pawnbroker's own past.
The Archivist never lies about the ledger, but may refuse to answer.
The Memory Broker never gives information without naming a price first.

Transcript:
[0] The Pawnbroker: The bell over the shop door rings once, and the Pawnbroker looks up from the ledger without hurry. The figure in the doorway is dressed too well for this street, and carries a sealed writ the way other people carry a weapon.

"We're closed," the Pawnbroker says, and turns a page. "Unless you've come to pawn something. In which case we're open, and I'll want to know how many years, and whether you've pawned them before."

The writ slides across the counter. The Pawnbroker does not touch it yet. Outside, the city's memory-lamps gutter in the rain, and somewhere down the street a debt collector is calling in someone's childhood.
[1] The Queen's Agent: The bell over the shop door does not ring so much as sigh. The woman who steps in is dressed for the court but stands like someone who has spent years in rooms where the wrong word costs a year of your life.

She sets a sealed writ on the counter between you, and beside it a purse that is far too light for the errand she is about to describe.

"You are the pawnbroker," she says. It is not a question. "The crown has a debt to collect, and the ledger says you are the only hand in this city that can reach it."

Her eyes move once around the shop — the shelves of stoppered years, the tags in your own handwriting — and come back to you.

"The queen's childhood was pawned. Years ago. It is no longer in one place, and it is no longer in the palace's keeping. I am here to commission its recovery." She folds her hands. "Name your terms, and I will tell you what the crown will and will not pay."
[2] Max Nightriver: I set down my loupe and break the seal on the writ. Whose ledger was the queen's childhood pawned against, and how many years does the crown think it is worth?
[3] The Pawnbroker: The Pawnbroker reads the writ in silence. Outside, rain drums against the shop shutters, and the memory-lamps along the street flicker. The Pawnbroker sets the paper flat on the counter and taps it once.
"Seven years. That's what the crown says it lost." The Pawnbroker's voice is flat, like a banker reciting a balance sheet. "Seven years of a girl's life, pawned before she could pronounce 'your majesty.' And as for the ledger—the original entry was made against a name that no longer exists. Or never existed."
The Pawnbroker glances at the agent. "The crown's own Keeper of Debts has been scrubbing the records. Some entries are gone entirely. Others are broken into pieces, traded like coin, diluted with each transfer. One piece is in the hands of a merchant-prince's daughter. Another is held by a memory-broker who specializes in first kisses. And the largest fragment is still in the Keeper's own vault, under a name that doesn't match the queen's."
The Pawnbroker slides the writ back across the counter. "You're not asking for a retrieval. You're asking for a puzzle to be solved. And every piece that comes back won't be the piece that left. A memory returned after years in circulation is like a coin that's been worn thin. The edges are frayed. The details are blurred."
The Pawnbroker pauses, and for a moment their eyes wander to the shelves of stoppered jars. "The crown pays in gold and titles. I don't care about either. But I do care about the ledger. If I find these years, I'll want a share of the memory for the shop's collection. A small piece. Just to see what a queen's childhood tastes like."
[4] The Queen's Agent: "Seven years," the agent says softly. "That was the price of a father's salvation, and a daughter's silence."
She lets that slip, then catches it, her expression as smooth as court marble.
"The crown is prepared to allow you a share of the retrieval. A single month from the recovered years, entered into your ledger under the shop's name. That is my final offer." She does not blink. "The remaining months must be restored to the palace, piece by piece. And you will find that some of these fragments are held by people who would rather the queen forget entirely."
She produces a second sheet from her cloak, this one not sealed, but marked with three names in ink so black it seems to pull at the light.
"Start here. The daughter of Merchant-Prince Voss holds the first fragment: a summer afternoon in the palace gardens, age four. She is sentimental, and she values rarity over coin. She will likely accept a trade, but only if the offering is as precious as the memory itself." The agent slides the paper across the counter. "And a warning—the woman who holds the second piece is the very broker who brokered the first. She knows the shape of the debt in a way others do not. Be cautious. This is not merely a collection. It is an unmaking."
[5] Max Nightriver: A month is an insult. Show me the original pawn ticket, or tell me which district's ledger I should start with.
[6] The Pawnbroker: The Queen's Agent: The agent's jaw tightens, a flicker of frustration breaking through the polished mask. She looks at the list on the counter, then at the Pawnbroker.
"The original ticket is in the Keeper of Debts' private vault. If you want to see it, you will have to make an appointment with the woman who spends her nights editing the crown's history. I suggest you don't." Her voice drops, barely above a whisper. "The Keeper does not like being reminded of things she has tried to forget."
She taps the list with one finger. "The daughter of Merchant-Prince Voss lives in the Jade District, where the wealthy hoard memories like pearls. The memory-broker, the woman who handled the original transaction, operates from the Low Markets in the Silk District. And the third fragment, the largest one, is still being held in the crown's own Debt Hall. The Keeper is keeping it under lock and key, listed under the false name."
The agent's eyes search the Pawnbroker's face. "A month's share is the price for the risk. You will have to infiltrate the Jade District's social circles, negotiate with a broker who has seen every kind of desperation, and—if you are truly foolish—attempt to extract information from the crown's most dangerous servant."
She folds her arms. "If you want a higher price, you'll have to explain why you're worth it. Tell me what you have that can buy seven years of a queen's life back from the shadows."

[0] The Pawnbroker: The bell over the shop door rings once, and the Pawnbroker looks up from the ledger without hurry. The figure in the doorway is dressed too well for this street, and carries a sealed writ the way other people carry a weapon.

"We're closed," the Pawnbroker says, and turns a page. "Unless you've come to pawn something. In which case we're open, and I'll want to know how many years, and whether you've pawned them before."

The writ slides across the counter. The Pawnbroker does not touch it yet. Outside, the city's memory-lamps gutter in the rain, and somewhere down the street a debt collector is calling in someone's childhood.
[1] The Queen's Agent: The bell over the shop door does not ring so much as sigh. The woman who steps in is dressed for the court but stands like someone who has spent years in rooms where the wrong word costs a year of your life.

She sets a sealed writ on the counter between you, and beside it a purse that is far too light for the errand she is about to describe.

"You are the pawnbroker," she says. It is not a question. "The crown has a debt to collect, and the ledger says you are the only hand in this city that can reach it."

Her eyes move once around the shop — the shelves of stoppered years, the tags in your own handwriting — and come back to you.

"The queen's childhood was pawned. Years ago. It is no longer in one place, and it is no longer in the palace's keeping. I am here to commission its recovery." She folds her hands. "Name your terms, and I will tell you what the crown will and will not pay."
[2] Max Nightriver: I set down my loupe and break the seal on the writ. Whose ledger was the queen's childhood pawned against, and how many years does the crown think it is worth?
[3] The Pawnbroker: The Pawnbroker reads the writ in silence. Outside, rain drums against the shop shutters, and the memory-lamps along the street flicker. The Pawnbroker sets the paper flat on the counter and taps it once.
"Seven years. That's what the crown says it lost." The Pawnbroker's voice is flat, like a banker reciting a balance sheet. "Seven years of a girl's life, pawned before she could pronounce 'your majesty.' And as for the ledger—the original entry was made against a name that no longer exists. Or never existed."
The Pawnbroker glances at the agent. "The crown's own Keeper of Debts has been scrubbing the records. Some entries are gone entirely. Others are broken into pieces, traded like coin, diluted with each transfer. One piece is in the hands of a merchant-prince's daughter. Another is held by a memory-broker who specializes in first kisses. And the largest fragment is still in the Keeper's own vault, under a name that doesn't match the queen's."
The Pawnbroker slides the writ back across the counter. "You're not asking for a retrieval. You're asking for a puzzle to be solved. And every piece that comes back won't be the piece that left. A memory returned after years in circulation is like a coin that's been worn thin. The edges are frayed. The details are blurred."
The Pawnbroker pauses, and for a moment their eyes wander to the shelves of stoppered jars. "The crown pays in gold and titles. I don't care about either. But I do care about the ledger. If I find these years, I'll want a share of the memory for the shop's collection. A small piece. Just to see what a queen's childhood tastes like."
[4] The Queen's Agent: "Seven years," the agent says softly. "That was the price of a father's salvation, and a daughter's silence."
She lets that slip, then catches it, her expression as smooth as court marble.
"The crown is prepared to allow you a share of the retrieval. A single month from the recovered years, entered into your ledger under the shop's name. That is my final offer." She does not blink. "The remaining months must be restored to the palace, piece by piece. And you will find that some of these fragments are held by people who would rather the queen forget entirely."
She produces a second sheet from her cloak, this one not sealed, but marked with three names in ink so black it seems to pull at the light.
"Start here. The daughter of Merchant-Prince Voss holds the first fragment: a summer afternoon in the palace gardens, age four. She is sentimental, and she values rarity over coin. She will likely accept a trade, but only if the offering is as precious as the memory itself." The agent slides the paper across the counter. "And a warning—the woman who holds the second piece is the very broker who brokered the first. She knows the shape of the debt in a way others do not. Be cautious. This is not merely a collection. It is an unmaking."
[5] Max Nightriver: A month is an insult. Show me the original pawn ticket, or tell me which district's ledger I should start with.
[6] The Pawnbroker: The Queen's Agent: The agent's jaw tightens, a flicker of frustration breaking through the polished mask. She looks at the list on the counter, then at the Pawnbroker.
"The original ticket is in the Keeper of Debts' private vault. If you want to see it, you will have to make an appointment with the woman who spends her nights editing the crown's history. I suggest you don't." Her voice drops, barely above a whisper. "The Keeper does not like being reminded of things she has tried to forget."
She taps the list with one finger. "The daughter of Merchant-Prince Voss lives in the Jade District, where the wealthy hoard memories like pearls. The memory-broker, the woman who handled the original transaction, operates from the Low Markets in the Silk District. And the third fragment, the largest one, is still being held in the crown's own Debt Hall. The Keeper is keeping it under lock and key, listed under the false name."
The agent's eyes search the Pawnbroker's face. "A month's share is the price for the risk. You will have to infiltrate the Jade District's social circles, negotiate with a broker who has seen every kind of desperation, and—if you are truly foolish—attempt to extract information from the crown's most dangerous servant."
She folds her arms. "If you want a higher price, you'll have to explain why you're worth it. Tell me what you have that can buy seven years of a queen's life back from the shadows."
[7] The Queen's Agent: *The agent's face remains impassive, though there is a cold stillness to her posture that suggests she has considered the word 'insult' and found it wanting.*
"The original pawn ticket is not mine to give," *she says, her voice measured.* "It rests in the Keeper of Debts' private vault, where it has remained for years. The palace does not part with such things lightly—nor with its secrets."
*She leans forward slightly, her tone shifting from command to something more like a confidence shared in the shadow of the counter.* "If you seek a starting point, begin with the Silk District. Mira Vane, the broker there, has handled more pawned childhoods than most citizens have had years of their own. She will not give you names freely, but she will tell you which houses are trading in royal fragments and what currencies they accept."
*The agent pauses, her gaze unwavering.* "And as for the price—you mistake the offer for a wage. It is not. A month's share of a queen's childhood is a commodity of immense value in the memory market. But the true payment for this commission is something else entirely."
*She straightens, returning to her formal bearing.* "When the years are recovered, your name will be stricken from every ledger-house in this city. Your debts—public, private, and secret—will be erased. You will walk the streets as no one else does: with a clean slate."

Transcript:
[0] The Pawnbroker: The bell over the shop door rings once, and the Pawnbroker looks up from the ledger without hurry. The figure in the doorway is dressed too well for this street, and carries a sealed writ the way other people carry a weapon.

"We're closed," the Pawnbroker says, and turns a page. "Unless you've come to pawn something. In which case we're open, and I'll want to know how many years, and whether you've pawned them before."

The writ slides across the counter. The Pawnbroker does not touch it yet. Outside, the city's memory-lamps gutter in the rain, and somewhere down the street a debt collector is calling in someone's childhood.
[1] The Queen's Agent: The bell over the shop door does not ring so much as sigh. The woman who steps in is dressed for the court but stands like someone who has spent years in rooms where the wrong word costs a year of your life.

She sets a sealed writ on the counter between you, and beside it a purse that is far too light for the errand she is about to describe.

"You are the pawnbroker," she says. It is not a question. "The crown has a debt to collect, and the ledger says you are the only hand in this city that can reach it."

Her eyes move once around the shop — the shelves of stoppered years, the tags in your own handwriting — and come back to you.

"The queen's childhood was pawned. Years ago. It is no longer in one place, and it is no longer in the palace's keeping. I am here to commission its recovery." She folds her hands. "Name your terms, and I will tell you what the crown will and will not pay."
[2] Max Nightriver: I set down my loupe and break the seal on the writ. Whose ledger was the queen's childhood pawned against, and how many years does the crown think it is worth?
[3] The Pawnbroker: The Pawnbroker reads the writ in silence. Outside, rain drums against the shop shutters, and the memory-lamps along the street flicker. The Pawnbroker sets the paper flat on the counter and taps it once.
"Seven years. That's what the crown says it lost." The Pawnbroker's voice is flat, like a banker reciting a balance sheet. "Seven years of a girl's life, pawned before she could pronounce 'your majesty.' And as for the ledger—the original entry was made against a name that no longer exists. Or never existed."
The Pawnbroker glances at the agent. "The crown's own Keeper of Debts has been scrubbing the records. Some entries are gone entirely. Others are broken into pieces, traded like coin, diluted with each transfer. One piece is in the hands of a merchant-prince's daughter. Another is held by a memory-broker who specializes in first kisses. And the largest fragment is still in the Keeper's own vault, under a name that doesn't match the queen's."
The Pawnbroker slides the writ back across the counter. "You're not asking for a retrieval. You're asking for a puzzle to be solved. And every piece that comes back won't be the piece that left. A memory returned after years in circulation is like a coin that's been worn thin. The edges are frayed. The details are blurred."
The Pawnbroker pauses, and for a moment their eyes wander to the shelves of stoppered jars. "The crown pays in gold and titles. I don't care about either. But I do care about the ledger. If I find these years, I'll want a share of the memory for the shop's collection. A small piece. Just to see what a queen's childhood tastes like."
[4] The Queen's Agent: "Seven years," the agent says softly. "That was the price of a father's salvation, and a daughter's silence."
She lets that slip, then catches it, her expression as smooth as court marble.
"The crown is prepared to allow you a share of the retrieval. A single month from the recovered years, entered into your ledger under the shop's name. That is my final offer." She does not blink. "The remaining months must be restored to the palace, piece by piece. And you will find that some of these fragments are held by people who would rather the queen forget entirely."
She produces a second sheet from her cloak, this one not sealed, but marked with three names in ink so black it seems to pull at the light.
"Start here. The daughter of Merchant-Prince Voss holds the first fragment: a summer afternoon in the palace gardens, age four. She is sentimental, and she values rarity over coin. She will likely accept a trade, but only if the offering is as precious as the memory itself." The agent slides the paper across the counter. "And a warning—the woman who holds the second piece is the very broker who brokered the first. She knows the shape of the debt in a way others do not. Be cautious. This is not merely a collection. It is an unmaking."
[5] Max Nightriver: A month is an insult. Show me the original pawn ticket, or tell me which district's ledger I should start with.
[6] The Pawnbroker: The Queen's Agent: The agent's jaw tightens, a flicker of frustration breaking through the polished mask. She looks at the list on the counter, then at the Pawnbroker.
"The original ticket is in the Keeper of Debts' private vault. If you want to see it, you will have to make an appointment with the woman who spends her nights editing the crown's history. I suggest you don't." Her voice drops, barely above a whisper. "The Keeper does not like being reminded of things she has tried to forget."
She taps the list with one finger. "The daughter of Merchant-Prince Voss lives in the Jade District, where the wealthy hoard memories like pearls. The memory-broker, the woman who handled the original transaction, operates from the Low Markets in the Silk District. And the third fragment, the largest one, is still being held in the crown's own Debt Hall. The Keeper is keeping it under lock and key, listed under the false name."
The agent's eyes search the Pawnbroker's face. "A month's share is the price for the risk. You will have to infiltrate the Jade District's social circles, negotiate with a broker who has seen every kind of desperation, and—if you are truly foolish—attempt to extract information from the crown's most dangerous servant."
She folds her arms. "If you want a higher price, you'll have to explain why you're worth it. Tell me what you have that can buy seven years of a queen's life back from the shadows."
[7] The Queen's Agent: *The agent's face remains impassive, though there is a cold stillness to her posture that suggests she has considered the word 'insult' and found it wanting.*
"The original pawn ticket is not mine to give," *she says, her voice measured.* "It rests in the Keeper of Debts' private vault, where it has remained for years. The palace does not part with such things lightly—nor with its secrets."
*She leans forward slightly, her tone shifting from command to something more like a confidence shared in the shadow of the counter.* "If you seek a starting point, begin with the Silk District. Mira Vane, the broker there, has handled more pawned childhoods than most citizens have had years of their own. She will not give you names freely, but she will tell you which houses are trading in royal fragments and what currencies they accept."
*The agent pauses, her gaze unwavering.* "And as for the price—you mistake the offer for a wage. It is not. A month's share of a queen's childhood is a commodity of immense value in the memory market. But the true payment for this commission is something else entirely."
*She straightens, returning to her formal bearing.* "When the years are recovered, your name will be stricken from every ledger-house in this city. Your debts—public, private, and secret—will be erased. You will walk the streets as no one else does: with a clean slate."
